newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan envoy sets damage-control trip to S.Africa.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan envoy sets damage-control trip to S.Africa.

text.p: Taiwan's foreign minister said on Friday he would leave soon for South Africa to try to limit the political damage from Pretoria's plan to sever diplomatic ties with Taiwan in favour of communist China.
"I originally planned to go to South Africa in January, but now I am advancing my schedule. The South African side is aware of my decision," Foreign Minister John Chang told state radio.
"I plan to leave for South Africa within a very short period of time, probably within one week," Chang said.
Chang said he planned to open negotiations with senior officials there.
"I hope we can maintain maximum contacts between the two countries," he said.

South African President Nelson Mandela said on Wednesday that Pretoria, a longtime diplomatic ally of Taiwan's, would switch diplomatic ties to Beijing by the end of 1997 in a move that caused shock in increasingly isolated Taiwan.

About a dozen Taiwanese on Friday staged a brief, peaceful demonstration at the South African embassy in Taipei, which stood in sharp contrast to the angry and sometimes violent protests that followed the severing of ties by the United States in 1978 and South Korea in 1992.
"Two people entered the embassy to deliver a protest letter. It lasted only about 15 minutes," an eyewitness said.
Taiwan's ambassador to South Africa Loh I-Cheng said on Thursday he had lodged a very strong protest with Mandela's government.
Loh said he had been given only 28 hours notice of the diplomatic shift and was surprised by what he called Pretoria's "unusual" way of handling the move.
South African ex-President F.W. de Klerk slammed Mandela's decision, saying the government had betrayed a good friend.

South Africa is the biggest of only 30 countries -- mostly underdeveloped states in central America and Africa -- that recognise Taiwan's Republic of China government rather than the communist People's Republic of China on the mainland.
Taiwan and China have been separated politically since a civil war ended in 1949. Both governments say they want reunification but disagree on the terms.
China sees Taiwan as a renegade province not entitled to foreign ties, while Taiwan insists its 21 million people have a right to international representation.
